newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Business only on Kohl's flying Brazil visit.
newsitem.headline: Business only on Kohl's flying Brazil visit.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl was due to arrive in Brazil on Tuesday, travelling through three Latin American countries without any Cabinet ministers but with a pack of prominent German businessmen in tow.

Kohl, arriving from Argentina and flying to Mexico next, will spend barely 24 hours in Brasilia but officials said his agenda would be packed and the German executives with him would be fed a heavy dose of information on the Brazilian economy.

Relations began with German immigration at the beginning of the 19th century. The colonists, enticed to Brazil when slavery started going out of fashion, settled mainly in the southern states, where the climate most resembles that of Europe.
A wane in ties during and after the Second World War, when Brazil joined the Allies to fight the Nazis, was followed by a flood of investments during the 1960s and 1970s.
Since then, German giants like carmakers Volkswagen and Mercedes-Benz and electronics firm Siemens have established themselves as major players in Brazil.

The company bosses travelling with Kohl were coming to check on their investments and take advantage of the "open doors" that several recent visits by German Cabinet ministers have left in their wake, in particular August's tour of Brazil by German Telecommunications Minister Wolfgang Boetsch.
"Brazil is in now. Everybody wants to come here," the German diplomat said.
Kohl, who meets President Fernando Henrique Cardoso shortly after landing, was expected to sign an accord on technical cooperation and a memorandum of understanding on transport.

"The visit will be very intense," said Marcelo Jardim, head of the Brazilian Foreign Ministry's Europe Department. "It is extremely important. Kohl is visiting the three Latin American countries where the most important German investments are."

Jardim said the 12 German company bosses travelling with Kohl were "heavyweights". Finance Minister Pedro Malan was due to brief them on the state of the Brazilian economy less than two hours after they land.
Kohl himself was expected to meet leaders of the Brazilian business community Wednesday morning for a working breakfast and some "serious talk" about investment, Jardim told reporters.

Germany is the second largest foreign investor in Brazil, sporting a portfolio that amounted to $7.0 billion in 1995. It is also Brazil's third most important trading partner with some $7.0 billion in bilateral trade a year.

German diplomatic sources said Kohl's brief stop-off, coming after an official visit in 1991 and participation in the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro, showed that Bonn took Latin America seriously.
Launched several years ago with much fanfare, Germany's "Latin America Concept", an economic policy statement on the region, was at first taken with a pinch of salt.
But with economic stability gaining ground, German commercial interest in Latin America has surged, though it still trails behind the importance of Asia's burgeoning economies.
"Of the three, Argentina, Mexico and Brazil, Brazil is undoubtedly the most important," a German diplomat said, requesting anonymity.
Ties between Europe's economic powerhouse and Latin America's largest economy have been traditionally tight.
